title: Multiplying and dividing fractions
summary: Use bars to see that multiplying by a fraction means "how many lots" or "what fraction of", and dividing by a fraction means "how many fit".
guide: Multiplying a whole number by a fraction means taking that fraction several times: 3 × {{frac:2/5}} means three lots of {{frac:2/5}}.
{{frac:1/2}} of {{frac:2/3}} means half of two thirds. On the grid bar, the striped columns show {{frac:2/3}}. Use + and − to split the bar into rows, then shade cells.
Dividing by a fraction asks "how many of this fraction fit into that number?" That is why the answer can be bigger than the number you started with.

three-lots.title: Three lots of two fifths
three-lots.prompt: 3 × {{frac:2/5}} means three lots of {{frac:2/5}}. First, predict: will the answer be more or less than one whole? Then shade three lots of {{frac:2/5}} on these two bars.
three-lots.hint: Shade 2 fifths at a time. When the first bar is full, carry on in the second bar.
three-lots.success: Well done! 3 lots of 2 fifths is 6 fifths: 3 × {{frac:2/5}} = {{frac:6/5}}, which is {{mixed:1 1/5}}.
three-lots.why: In 3 × {{frac:2/5}}, why is only the numerator multiplied by 3, while the denominator stays 5?
three-lots.model: The denominator 5 tells you the size of each part: one fifth. Taking 2 fifths three times gives 3 times as many parts (6 of them), but each part is still one fifth. So the answer is {{frac:6/5}}, which is more than one whole: one full bar and {{frac:1/5}}.

feedback.too-small: Not enough yet. Three lots of {{frac:2/5}} is 6 fifths. When the first bar is full, carry on in the second bar.
feedback.too-big: That's too much. Three lots of 2 parts is 6 parts.
feedback.empty: You haven't shaded anything yet. Shade 2 parts, then 2 more, then 2 more.

half-of-two-thirds.title: Half of two thirds
half-of-two-thirds.prompt: The striped columns are {{frac:2/3}} of the bar. What fraction of the whole bar is {{frac:1/2}} of this {{frac:2/3}}? First, predict. Then use + to split the bar into 2 rows and shade half of the striped part.
half-of-two-thirds.hint: With 2 rows, the striped part is 4 cells. Half of it is 2 cells. How many cells does the whole bar have?
half-of-two-thirds.success: Great! 2 cells out of 6 are shaded: {{frac:1/2}} × {{frac:2/3}} = {{frac:2/6}}, which is the same as {{frac:1/3}}.
half-of-two-thirds.why: Why is the answer {{frac:2/6}}? Point to the 2 and the 6 on the bar. Why do you think the answer is smaller than {{frac:2/3}}?
half-of-two-thirds.model: The columns split the bar into 3, and the rows split each column into 2. So the whole bar has 3 × 2 = 6 cells: that's the denominator. The striped part is 2 columns, and half of it is 1 cell in each, so 2 × 1 = 2 cells: that's the numerator. That's why we multiply numerator by numerator and denominator by denominator. The answer is smaller because we only took half of {{frac:2/3}}, and half of something is less than the whole of it.

feedback.wrong-denominator: That's the right amount! But this time show it with rows: use + to split the bar into 2 rows, then shade half of the striped part.
feedback.too-big: That's too much. Shade only half of the striped part, not all of it.
feedback.too-small: Not enough. Shade half of the striped part: one cell in each striped column.
feedback.empty: You haven't shaded any cells yet. First use + to split the bar into 2 rows.

share-three-quarters.title: Three quarters shared by three
share-three-quarters.prompt: {{frac:3/4}} of a cake is left (the striped columns). Three friends share it equally: {{frac:3/4}} ÷ 3. First, predict what fraction of the whole cake each friend gets. Then shade one friend's share.
share-three-quarters.hint: The striped part has 3 pieces and there are 3 friends. How many pieces does each friend get?
share-three-quarters.success: That's right! Each friend gets {{frac:1/4}} of the cake: {{frac:3/4}} ÷ 3 = {{frac:1/4}}
share-three-quarters.why: If the same {{frac:3/4}} of the cake were shared by 2 friends, how much would each get? Use the rows on the bar to explain.
share-three-quarters.model: You can't share 3 quarter-pieces equally between 2. But if you split the bar into 2 rows, the whole bar has 8 cells and the striped part has 6. Each friend gets 3 cells, which is {{frac:3/8}}. Dividing by 2 is the same as taking half: {{frac:3/4}} ÷ 2 = {{frac:1/2}} × {{frac:3/4}} = {{frac:3/8}}

feedback.too-big: That's more than one friend's share. Share the striped part between 3 and shade just one share.
feedback.too-small: That's less than one friend's share. Share the striped part between 3; all of the cake should be shared, with nothing left over.
feedback.empty: You haven't shaded anything yet. Shade one friend's share.

quarters-in-two.title: How many quarters are in 2?
quarters-in-two.prompt: 2 ÷ {{frac:1/4}} means "how many {{frac:1/4}}s fit into 2 wholes?" First, predict: is the answer bigger or smaller than 2? Then use + to split both bars into quarters and count them.
quarters-in-two.hint: Split each bar into 4 parts. One bar has 4 quarters. How many do two bars have?
quarters-in-two.success: Well done! 8 quarters fit into 2 wholes: 2 ÷ {{frac:1/4}} = 8
quarters-in-two.why: Dividing usually makes a number smaller. Why is 2 ÷ {{frac:1/4}} much bigger than 2?
quarters-in-two.model: Division asks "how many of these fit into that?" When you divide by a number smaller than 1, each piece is smaller than a whole, so more than one piece fits into each whole. Each whole holds 4 quarters, so 2 wholes hold 2 × 4 = 8. That's why dividing by {{frac:1/4}} is the same as multiplying by 4, the {{term:reciprocal}} of {{frac:1/4}}. The smaller the piece, the more of them fit.

feedback.too-small: Not enough. Count the quarters in both bars.
feedback.too-big: Too many. Split each bar into exactly 4 parts and count the parts.
feedback.empty: Type a number: how many quarters did you count?
